name: Northeast Sahaptin
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Jacobs, Melville. 1931. A sketch of Northern Sahaptin grammar. Univ. of Washington Publications in Anthropology 4(2) (covers NE dialects incl. Walla Walla)

new_statements.quote: Nez Perce and Sahaptin are syllable timed languages with three levels of stress. The orthographic traditions of both languages mark only primary stress with a secondary stress being considered more or less predictable. In Sahaptin all lexical morphemes have morpheme inherent stress. [...] Morphemes with inherent stress follow a stress hierarchy (suffix ⊂ prefix ⊂ root): (93) S itkʷáta /i-tkʷáta/ 'he has eaten' (94) S pátkʷata /pá-tkʷáta/ 'he has eaten it' (95) S patkʷatałá /pá-tkʷáta-łá/ 'cannibal'
new_statements.citation: Rude, Noel. 2012. Reconstructing Proto-Sahaptian sounds. Papers for the 47th International Conference on Salish and Neighbouring Languages (University of British Columbia Working Papers in Linguistics 32), 292-324.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2 'Stress', p. 302 (first three sentences) and p. 304 (hierarchy sentence with exx. 93-95); pdf pages 11 and 13
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (33 pp., text layer with custom font encoding that garbles accented characters, so I rendered pdf pp. 11-13 = printed pp. 302-304 to images and read them). Printed p. 302, sec. '2 Stress', first sentences read exactly: 'Nez Perce and Sahaptin are syllable timed languages with three levels of stress. The orthographic traditions of both languages mark only primary stress with a secondary stress being considered more or less predictable. In Sahaptin all lexical morphemes have morpheme inherent stress. Some Nez [p.303] Perce words also have morpheme inherent stress...'. Printed p. 304: 'Morphemes with inherent stress follow a stress hierarchy (suffix ⊂ prefix ⊂ root): (93) S itkʷá…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexical: every root/lexical morpheme carries its own inherent stress on an unpredictable syllable, and some affixes are inherently stressed; in a complex word a single primary stress surfaces on the highest-ranked stressed morpheme (stressed suffix beats stressed prefix beats root). No positional default (contrast Nez Perce penult rule, Rude 2006:272).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rude 2012: three levels of stress, secondary 'considered more or less predictable', not described. Jacobs 1931:117 (snippet): in the 'Umatilla reservation dialects' (Umatilla, Walla Walla) 'there may be two, three or four accented syllables to a word, each accent gentle... the rules for stress in these dialects are quite elaborate', versus one accent per word in NW Sahaptin; Hargus & Beavert 2014 fn.16 report Rude (1988) suggesting secondary stresses in Sahaptin.
new_statements.exceptions: Function words/clitics unstressed (Jacobs 1931:117: connective ku- and pronominal enclitics never stressed; Hargus & Beavert for Yakima). Hargus & Beavert (Yakima) add 'strong roots' that keep stress against prefixes; not stated for NE.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress in citation/orthographic forms (acute accent); statement is for Sahaptin as a whole (all three dialect clusters), with Umatilla as the default source of examples and NE (Walla Walla) forms cited alongside; no NE-specific stress rule is given.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Rude 2012) is made for Sahaptin as a whole -- Rude defines Sahaptin as three dialect clusters incl. Northeast (Priest Rapids/Wanapam, Walla Walla, Palouse) and credits a Walla Walla speaker (Elizabeth Wocatsie Jones) for the NE forms, but his default examples are Umatilla (umat1237, Columbia River Sahaptin). No NE-specific (wall1238) stress description could be opened. Jacobs 1931:117 (snippet only) treats Walla Walla together with Umatilla as the 'Umatilla reservation dialects', which he says differ prosodically from NW Sahaptin (yaki1237 etc.) in allowing several gentle accents per word. All detailed modern stress work (Hargus & Beavert; Jansen 2010) is on Yakima = Northwest Sahaptin.

sources.note: Sec. 2 'Stress', pp. 302-304 (page images read): Sahaptin (defined p. 292 as three dialect clusters: Columbia River, Northwest, Northeast = Priest Rapids, Walla Walla, Palouse) has three levels of stress, only primary marked; 'In Sahaptin all lexical morphemes have morpheme inherent stress'; 'Morphemes with inherent stress follow a stress hierarchy (suffix > prefix > root)' with exx. i-tkʷáta 'he has eaten', pá-tkʷata, patkʷatałá 'cannibal'. Sahaptin examples default to Umatilla; NE forms credited to Walla Walla speaker Elizabeth Wocatsie Jones.

sources.citation: Hargus, Sharon & Virginia Beavert. 2014. Northwest Sahaptin. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 44(3): 319-342.
sources.note: Yakima (NW Sahaptin) only: accent contrastive with minimal pairs (pámta/pamtá), accented affixes outrank roots, correlates pitch+energy; fn.1 lists the Northeast dialects (Walla Walla, Wanapam, Palouse, Lower Snake); fn.16 'Rude (1988) suggested that there may be secondary stresses in Sahaptin'; quotes Jacobs 1931:117.

sources.citation: Jansen, Joana. 2010. A grammar of Yakima Ichishkíin/Sahaptin. PhD dissertation, University of Oregon.
sources.note: Yakima only (grep of sec. 2.6): word-level stress, one primary stress per word, not entirely predictable, stress-stealing affixes; cites Rude 1988b 'A report from the field' as unpublished UO ms.

sources.citation: Rude, Noel. 2006. Proto-Sahaptian vocalism. Papers for ICSNL 41 (UBCWPL 18), 264-277.
sources.note: p. 272: 'Though there are patterns, stress is morpheme inherent in Sahaptin in so far as there is no universally applicable principle such as the penultimate stress rule in Nez Perce.' Pan-Sahaptin, comparative.

sources.citation: Hargus, Sharon & Virginia Beavert. 2016. Sahaptin: Between stress and tone. Proceedings of AMP 2015.
sources.note: Yakima: every lexical word has exactly one accent; root accent location unpredictable; realization hierarchy suffix < strong root < prefix < root; Umatilla briefly contrasted; nothing on NE dialects beyond the three-cluster classification (Jacobs 1931, Rigsby 1965).
